lessons.title: Tracking a Company's Working Capital Trend on screener.in

children.text: Everything in this chapter so far has been calculation. This lesson is navigation. In about ten minutes on screener.in you can pull twelve years of working capital history for any listed Indian company, spot the year something broke, and check whether it was fixed. You do not need a subscription, a terminal or a spreadsheet to start.
We will use Hindustan Unilever as the worked example, because its twelve-year record shows almost every pattern you will ever need to recognise.
Open screener.in, search for a company, and you land on its page. Two decisions come first.

columns.label: Consolidated or standalone
points: The toggle sits near the top of the company page
Consolidated includes subsidiaries and joint ventures
Standalone covers only the parent entity
Use consolidated for any group with meaningful subsidiaries
Whichever you pick, use the same basis for every peer you compare

columns.label: Which section to open
points: Balance Sheet gives you the rupee totals, though current items are grouped
Ratios gives you the days figures already computed
Cash Flows shows the annual working capital movement in rupees
Quarterly Results catches strain that an annual figure hides
Documents links to the annual reports where the ageing notes live

body.caption: What each row in the Ratios section is telling you

cells: How long customers take to pay
A steady climb while sales are flat, which means collections are slipping
How long stock sits before it sells
A jump with no matching sales growth, which usually means unsold product
How long the company takes to pay suppliers
A sharp rise, which can mean either new bargaining power or a cash crunch
Inventory plus debtor minus payable days
The direction over five years, not the level in any one year
The broader net working capital measure
A wide or widening gap against the cash conversion cycle
Whether a longer cycle is dragging returns down with it

body.text: Screener computes these rows from standardised data, so a figure may differ slightly from one you calculate by hand off the annual report. That is expected and does not matter. What matters is that the same method is applied to every year and every company, which makes the series comparable.

children.text: Reading Twelve Years of One Company
Here is what the Ratios section shows for Hindustan Unilever, consolidated, from FY2015 to FY2026. Every figure is in days.

body.title: Hindustan Unilever: cycle components, FY2015 to FY2026 (days)
Hindustan Unilever: cash conversion cycle vs working capital days

children.text: Read the story rather than the numbers. Payable days climbed from 148 in FY2015 to 185 in FY2018, and the cycle reached its most negative point of -107 days in that year. Then payable days fell back sharply to 123 by FY2023 and the cycle weakened to -50 days, its least negative in the whole series. From there, supplier terms lengthened again and the cycle recovered to -89 days by FY2026.

Underneath that, one line drifts quietly in the other direction. Debtor days went from 12 in FY2015 to 23 in FY2025, before easing to 19. For a company that collects from distributors almost on delivery, an eleven-day drift over a decade is worth a question, even though the overall cycle stayed comfortably negative throughout.

body.label: The pattern to take away
body.context: HUL's cycle ranged from -107 to -50 days across twelve years without the business ever being in difficulty. Any single year read in isolation would have told you almost nothing.

body.title: What does the FY2023 dip tell you?
body.question: HUL's cash conversion cycle weakened from about -107 days in FY2018 to about -50 days in FY2023, driven mainly by payable days falling from 185 to 123. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The company was running out of cash and could not pay suppliers
It was paying suppliers faster, which consumes cash but says nothing on its own about distress
Its customers had started paying much more slowly
The figures must be wrong, since a negative cycle cannot change that much
body.explanation: Shorter payable days mean money leaves sooner. That absorbs cash, but by itself it is not a distress signal: it can follow a change in supplier mix, sourcing terms, or a deliberate move to faster payment for better prices. Debtor days moved only from 13 to 19 over the same period, so customers were not the driver. To judge it properly you would read the cash flow statement and the management commentary.

children.text: Four Things the Trend Will Show You

stats.label: Direction
stats.context: A cycle lengthening every year is a warning long before any single year looks bad

stats.label: Divergence
stats.context: Receivable days rising while sales are flat means collection quality is slipping

stats.label: Composition
stats.value: Which of the three lines moved
stats.context: The same change in the cycle needs a different fix depending on its source

stats.label: Disagreement
stats.context: A wide gap means the action is outside the three trade lines

body.title: Three traps when reading screener data

children.text: Financial companies. Banks, non-banking financial companies and insurers have no meaningful inventory or trade payables, and their balance sheets are structured completely differently. Working capital ratios for them are noise. Skip these rows entirely.

Seasonality. Every figure is built from the 31 March balance sheet. A sugar mill, a fan manufacturer or a woollens brand can look very different in March than in October. Use the quarterly results section to see whether the year end is representative.

Consolidated versus standalone switches. If a company acquires a large subsidiary, its consolidated figures can jump for reasons that have nothing to do with operating discipline. Check whether the entity being reported changed before you conclude that the business did.

body.title: Convert a trend into rupees
body.prompt: A listed auto ancillary with annual sales of ₹800 crore improves its cash conversion cycle from 95 days to 78 days over two years. Roughly how much cash does that release, in ₹ crore? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: The cycle shortened by 17 days. One day of sales is ₹800 crore divided by 365, about ₹2.19 crore. Multiply by 17 days and the business frees up roughly ₹37 crore, permanently, without selling anything extra. This is the calculation that turns a ratios table into a boardroom conversation.

body.title: What to compare
body.textWithBlank: When comparing two companies on screener.in, always use the same basis for both, that is either consolidated or ___ figures, never one of each.
body.explanation: Mixing consolidated figures for one company with standalone figures for another makes the comparison meaningless, because the two cover different sets of entities.

body.title: Build a working capital view of any listed company in ten minutes
steps: Search the company on screener.in and choose consolidated unless the business is a single entity.
Scroll to the Ratios section and read Debtor Days, Inventory Days, Days Payable, Cash Conversion Cycle and Working Capital Days across all the years shown.
Note the best and worst years for the cycle, and which of the three components caused each move.
Compare the cycle trend with the sales growth line above it, to see whether days are rising while growth is not.
Check the gap between the cash conversion cycle and working capital days, and investigate the notes if it is wide.
Open the Cash Flows section and look at the working capital movement line, which converts those days into actual rupees.
Open the Peers section and repeat the exercise for two or three comparable companies on the same basis.
Open the latest annual report from the Documents section and read the receivables and inventory ageing notes for the final answer.

body.text: Screener gives you the question, never the answer. A cycle stretching by 30 days tells you something changed. Only the annual report notes, the management commentary and the quarterly numbers tell you what, and whether it is temporary.

body.title: The trend that needs explaining
body.scenario: You are reviewing a mid-cap packaging company on screener.in. Over five years its sales have grown from ₹620 crore to ₹1,040 crore. Debtor days went from 48 to 71, inventory days from 55 to 58, and days payable from 62 to 96. The cash conversion cycle moved from 41 days to 33 days, and management highlights the improved cycle in its annual report.
body.prompt: Is the improvement real? What would you check next, and in what order?
body.modelAnswer:
The headline cycle did improve by 8 days, but not for a good reason. Debtor days rose by 23 while inventory barely moved, and the whole improvement came from stretching suppliers by 34 days. The company is funding worsening collections with supplier credit.

What to check, in order. First, the receivables ageing note: how much of the book is over six months old, and how concentrated is it among a few customers? Second, the trade payables ageing note and the dues to micro and small enterprises line, because stretching suppliers beyond 45 days carries a statutory interest cost when those suppliers are registered MSMEs. Third, the cash flow statement, to see whether operating cash flow is keeping pace with reported profit. Fourth, short-term borrowings on the balance sheet, to see whether the limit is getting more fully drawn each year. Fifth, the quarterly results, to check whether the March position is representative.

What to conclude: the cycle improved, the business did not. A cycle that improves only because payables lengthened is borrowed time, not released cash.

children.text: Apply the same reading to the illustrative company from Chapter 1. Sunrise Ceramics' cycle went 62, 68, 71, 76, 80 days across five years. No single year looks alarming, and no benchmark was crossed. But the direction never changes, and 18 extra days at its scale is real money permanently absorbed into the business.

body.label: Hindustan Unilever ratios on screener.in
body.description: The twelve-year series used in this lesson. Scroll to the Ratios section and read the five working capital rows across every year shown.

body.label: Build your own screen
body.description: Screener lets you write conditions across its data fields and save the result as a screen, so you can filter listed companies on working capital measures and revisit the list later. Start from an existing public screen and edit it if you are new to the syntax.

points: Screener.in gives you a decade or more of working capital days for any listed Indian company at no cost, in the Ratios section.
Choose consolidated or standalone deliberately, and keep the same basis across every company you compare.
Read the trend and the composition, never a single year, because healthy companies swing widely across a decade.
Compare the days trend with sales growth: rising receivable days on flat sales is the classic early warning.
A wide gap between the cash conversion cycle and working capital days means the action is outside the three trade lines.
A cycle that improves only because payable days lengthened is not an improvement, it is borrowed funding.
Convert any change in days into rupees using daily sales, which is what turns the analysis into a decision.
